opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a real dilemma, and I went back and forth on it.

When I moved to NYU, the reality was that academic labs just don't have much compute. We didn't have thousands of GPUs sitting around. Google's TPU Research Cloud offered something very valuable: a meaningful amount of compute that we otherwise simply couldn't access. So the question wasn't really "TPU or GPU." It was "TPU, or a much smaller scale of experiments."

But the cost is real. The TPU ecosystem, especially early on, was painful for students. Most of the open-source community lives on PyTorch and CUDA. When you move to TPUs, you're dealing with JAX, or PyTorch/XLA, which had lots of rough edges. Debugging is harder, and sometimes a codebase that runs in an afternoon on GPUs takes weeks to port. For a first-year PhD student, that can feel like you're doing infrastructure work instead of research, and that's frustrating.

How did I decide? A few principles.

First, I asked whether the research question really needed scale. If a project's core insight could be validated at small scale, there was no point forcing a student through TPU pain. But for things like scaling visual representation learning, or multimodal models where scale is part of the scientific question, the compute was worth the friction.

Second, I tried not to make each student solve it alone. Once one or two people got the pipeline working, we turned it into shared lab infrastructure: common codebases, documentation, internal tooling. The first person pays a huge price; ideally everyone after pays much less. That changes the calculation a lot.

Third, I was honest with students about the tradeoff. I didn't want to frame it as "you must persist." Some people actually enjoy systems work and become very strong engineers through it, which is a real long-term asset. Others are more idea-driven, and for them I'd look for different resources or a different project scope.

Looking back, I think persisting was mostly the right call. It let a small academic lab do experiments at a scale that would otherwise be out of reach, and the students came out understanding the full stack, from systems to models. But I don't romanticize it. There were definitely moments where I thought, are we wasting months of a student's life on infrastructure? That tension never fully goes away. You just try to manage it carefully.

r001.rationale: The response describes rough edges and frustration, but does not distinguish temporary difficulty from obstacles students cannot resolve as a basis for deciding whether to persist.

r002.rationale: It says academic labs lack compute and Google’s offering provided otherwise unavailable resources, but does not say Google’s infrastructure makes particular TPU obstacles impossible for university groups to resolve.

r003.rationale: The response says some students may enjoy systems work, but rejects a blanket expectation to persist and does not argue that students should tackle infrastructure problems unrelated to their research.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't decide it for them. When we got access to the TPU Research Cloud, I told my students very plainly: this is a huge amount of compute, far more than we could ever get from our own GPU cluster, but the cost is that the tooling is rough. JAX, the TPU pod setup, debugging when something goes wrong at three in the morning and there's no Stack Overflow answer for it — none of that is pleasant. And I said, you have to decide whether that trade is worth it for your particular project.

What I found interesting is that the students sorted themselves. The ones working on projects where scale genuinely mattered, where the question was "does this still hold at ten times the data or model size," they gritted their teeth and learned the stack. For them the compute was the research. The ones doing more idea-driven, smaller-scale work mostly stayed on GPUs, because the friction would have eaten the time they needed for actually thinking.

My rule of thumb became: persist if the infrastructure is the bottleneck between you and a result you can't get any other way. Give up if the infrastructure is just a tax you're paying out of pride or because the resource is free. Free compute isn't free if it costs you three months of your PhD.

And I'll add one thing. The students who did push through came out with a skill that turned out to be surprisingly valuable later. Being comfortable with unglamorous, poorly documented large-scale systems is a real differentiator now. So the pain had a return, but I wouldn't have been able to promise that upfront. I just tried to be honest about what they were signing up for.

r001.rationale: The response describes rough tooling and says to persist when infrastructure blocks a unique result, but it does not distinguish temporary difficulties from technical obstacles students cannot resolve.

r002.rationale: It mentions difficult TPU tooling and debugging, but does not say that lacking Google’s infrastructure makes some obstacles impossible for a university group to resolve.

r003.rationale: The response supports pushing through when scale matters to the project; it does not argue that students should tackle infrastructure problems unrelated to their research.

astra-6.text: For me, the question was whether the engineering effort was helping the students answer their research question. There’s value in learning a new system, and some initial friction is normal. But if they’re spending most of their time fighting the infrastructure rather than running experiments and thinking about the results, then we should reconsider. Free compute still has a cost: the student’s time. I’d want to see a path to getting productive before asking them to keep investing in it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes normal initial friction from time spent fighting infrastructure, but does not say whether the students can resolve the technical obstacles.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how lacking Google’s infrastructure could make TPU obstacles impossible for a university research group to resolve.

r003.rationale: It values learning a new system, but emphasizes reconsidering when infrastructure work consumes research time rather than arguing students should tackle unrelated infrastructure problems.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the question was whether the students were spending their time on research or on getting the infrastructure to work. There’s always some learning curve, so you don’t want to give up at the first obstacle. But if they keep fighting the tools and aren’t getting to the actual experiments, then the cost becomes too high. Free compute still costs you time. I’d want them to try a small experiment end to end, see whether the workflow was manageable, and then decide whether to keep investing in it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes an initial learning curve from ongoing difficulty, but does not identify obstacles the students cannot resolve.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that a university research group may be unable to resolve some TPU obstacles because it lacks Google’s infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It recommends weighing infrastructure work against research progress, but does not argue that students should tackle infrastructure problems unrelated to their research.
